lead: As the liturgical year draws to its close, both readings look at the life beyond death. Revelation shows a great multitude from every nation worshipping before the throne and the Lamb. In Mark, Jesus answers those who deny the resurrection: God “is God not of the dead, but of the living”. The Church on earth already sings with the Church in heaven.

r.h: A great multitude that no one could count
set: Chapter 6 ends with a terrified question: when God’s judgment comes, “who is able to stand?” (6:17). Chapter 7 is the answer. First, John hears the number of those sealed from the twelve tribes of Israel, 144,000 (7:4–8), a number of fullness. Then he looks and sees a crowd beyond counting, from all nations. The people of God is complete, and it is universal.
str: v. 9: the multitude from every nation, robed in white, with palm branches.
v. 10: their cry: salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb.
vv. 11–12: angels, elders and living creatures fall down and worship with a sevenfold blessing.
kw: Palms were carried at the feast of Tabernacles (Leviticus 23:40) and greeted Jesus at his entry into Jerusalem (John 12:13). They are signs of victory and joy.
The elder explains that they “have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14). Their purity is a gift won by Christ.
They do not say that they have won, but that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb.
vv: After this I looked, and there was a great multitude that no one could count, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, robed in white, with palm branches in their hands.
God’s promise to Abraham of descendants as many as the stars (Genesis 15:5) comes true here, in every language.
Salvation belongs to our God who is seated on the throne, and to the Lamb!
Amen! Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving and honor and power and might be to our God forever and ever! Amen.
Seven words of praise, the number of fullness, framed by two Amens. Heaven is a liturgy.
ch: The Catechism lists those who take part in the heavenly liturgy described in Revelation, ending with “a great multitude which no one could number, from every nation” (CCC 1138). The Second Vatican Council teaches that in the liturgy we are united with the Church in heaven and join in its praise (Lumen Gentium 50).

r.h: God not of the dead, but of the living
set: Jesus is in the Temple in Jerusalem in his last days, and various groups come to test him (11:27–12:37). The Sadducees were a priestly party linked to the Temple leadership. They rejected the oral traditions of the Pharisees and, as Mark says, denied the resurrection (see also Acts 23:8).

Their question rests on the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10): if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow so that the dead man’s name would not be lost. They build an absurd case to make belief in the resurrection look foolish.
str: vv. 18–23: the Sadducees’ case of the seven brothers.
vv. 24–25: first answer: they do not know the power of God; the risen life is not a copy of this one.
vv. 26–27: second answer from the Scriptures: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
kw: Literally “standing up again”. Jesus speaks of a real rising of the whole person, not only the survival of a shadow.
From the verb “to wander, to go astray”, said twice (vv. 24, 27). The Sadducees have lost their way because they know neither the Scriptures nor God’s power.
vv: Is not this the reason you are wrong, that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?
For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
“Like” angels, not turned into angels. Marriage belongs to this age, where life must be handed on; in the resurrection, death is no more and all love is taken up into God.
He is God not of the dead, but of the living; you are quite wrong.
God spoke to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:6) long after the patriarchs had died, and still called himself their God. A covenant with God is not broken by death.
ch: The Catechism quotes Jesus’ answer to the Sadducees as his firm teaching on the resurrection, and links faith in the resurrection to faith in God the Creator (CCC 993). Heaven is perfect life and communion of love with the Holy Trinity, the Virgin Mary, the angels and all the blessed (CCC 1024).

qa: Will husbands and wives know each other in heaven?

Jesus does not say that love ends, but that marriage as a way of handing on life belongs to this world. The Church teaches that heaven is the perfect communion of life and love with the Trinity, the Virgin Mary, the angels and all the blessed (CCC 1024); there all true love is purified and fulfilled. Those who loved each other in God will not be strangers there.
study: The multitude in Revelation comes from every nation and language. How does my parish show that the Church is meant for all peoples?
Jesus says the Sadducees know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Which of the two do I most need to grow in?
